pinterest.title: Greek Orthodox Wedding Requirements: Who Can Marry, Papers and Dates
pinterest.description: Planning a Greek Orthodox wedding starts with your parish priest, not the venue. Under the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia's rules, confirm who can marry, which documents you need and which dates are closed, such as Great Lent until Easter Sunday and 1 to 15 August. The Notice of Intended Marriage and the Application to the Archdiocese are completed with the priest at least a month ahead, preferably three.

pinterest.title: Greek Orthodox Wedding Ceremony Explained: Rings, Crowns and Common Cup
pinterest.description: A Greek Orthodox wedding has two parts, the Betrothal and the Crowning, and no spoken vows. The rings are blessed and exchanged three times by the koumbaros, the priest joins your right hands, the stefana crown you both, you share the common cup, and the priest leads the Dance of Isaiah. Our guide walks through each step of the service as the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia sets it out.

pinterest.title: Greek Orthodox Wedding Documents: What the Parish Usually Asks For
pinterest.description: For a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia, each partner usually presents a birth certificate or passport and a baptismal certificate, plus a Certificate of Celibacy for an Orthodox partner never married before. Widowed and divorced partners need extra papers. These are the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia's requirements; marrying in Greece adds the local Metropolis, the municipality and the Australian Embassy in Athens.

slides: A Greek Orthodox wedding is a sacrament, not a ceremony you write yourselves. There are no spoken vows.
Start with your parish priest, before the venue or the save-the-date. Check that the Church can marry you, and that your date is open.

Under the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia's rules, a non-Orthodox partner must be a baptised Christian of a denomination the Church accepts, such as Roman Catholic, Anglican, Uniting, Lutheran or Presbyterian.
Closed dates in Australia include 13 December to Christmas Day, Great Lent until Easter Sunday, and 1 to 15 August. Easter moves each year, so confirm your calendar with your priest.
The Betrothal: the rings are blessed three times, and the koumbaros exchanges them between you three times.
The Crowning: the stefana are exchanged over your heads while the priest and chanter sing "Lord our God, crown them in glory and honour."
Then the common cup and the Dance of Isaiah, your first steps as a married couple.
Planning yours in Greece? Once your priest has confirmed the service, tell us your island and guest count, and a Wedded Advisor will talk through the venue, travel and vendors with you. Link in bio.
instagram_carousel.caption:
What actually happens at a Greek Orthodox wedding, and what has to happen first?

Our new guide explains the requirements and the ceremony, step by step. The church rules it covers are those of the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia, so if you are marrying elsewhere, ask your own parish priest which rules apply. In Greece, the local Metropolis sets the requirements.

The order of planning matters. Sit down with your parish priest before you hold a venue: check that the Church can marry you, and that your date is not one of the closed dates, such as Great Lent until Easter Sunday or 1 to 15 August.

The service itself has two parts. In the Betrothal, the rings are blessed and exchanged three times by the koumbaros or koumbara. In the Marriage Service, the priest joins your right hands, the stefana crown you both, you share the common cup, and the priest leads you in the Dance of Isaiah. Without the rings and the crowns, the wedding cannot begin.

A small detail for your photographer: there is no moment when you place the rings on each other's hands, so ask them to watch the sponsor's hands.

Dreaming of a chapel on the island where a grandparent was baptised? Send us a message with your island and guest count. Your Wedded Advisor is one person, start to finish, who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the service your priest confirms, and confirms inclusions in writing before you commit. Full guide at the link in our bio.
